author: M. P. Welch
title: North Carolina reactions highlight tensions after Charlie Kirk assassination - South Raleigh News
text:
Reactions in North Carolina to the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk have drawn attention to political tensions and responses from various public figures and institutions. The incident has sparked a range of comments, some critical of Kirk, from local officials and educators.
In Durham, the city’s Chief of Police posted on social media that Kirk “disguised himself as a Christian” and made claims about his views. This statement was supported by both the Mayor of Durham and members of the City Council.
In Pinebluff, Moore County, the town’s mayor called Kirk a racist and voiced criticism over a peaceful vigil organized in his memory.
Heidy Varner, a public school teacher in Trinity, was among several educators who commented publicly about Kirk. Varner accused him of “pushing hatred onto others,” along with other criticisms.
At UNC Wilmington, a mural painted on a spirit rock was defaced with colors associated with the transgender flag by individuals described as young socialist progressives.
A different outcome occurred in Winston-Salem after Rep. Pat Harrigan contacted Wake Forest University regarding an employee who said Kirk “had it coming.” The university subsequently terminated the employee’s position. Harrigan also indicated that Wake Forest would support establishing a Turning Point chapter on campus.
The press release states that these examples are not exhaustive and argues against what it calls efforts to silence discussion about activist behavior within the Democratic Party.
“The radical Left cannot erase the life and memory of Charlie Kirk. The movement he led to bring conservative values and involvement in politics directly to college campuses and beyond will reverberate for generations,” said NCGOP Communications Director Matt Mercer.
